newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate committee working on tax cut bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate committee working on tax cut bill.

text.p: The Senate Finance Committee worked Thursday on a bill that would cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years, with both Democrats and Republicans calling it a bipartisan effort.

The tone differed from last week's session in the House Ways and Means Committee, where Democrats offered their own tax plan and voted against the Republican bill. The House committee approved that legislation, and differences with the Senate version must eventually be worked out.
"As with any bipartisan effort, not everyone will be fully satisfied with this proposal," Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said.
"For my part, I would like to see greater tax relief, and I consider this the first in a series of steps that I hope will lead to deeper tax cuts and eventual long-term reform," he said.
Some Democrats said they preferred not to cut taxes at this time, but were obligated by last month's budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House.

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan of New York, the senior Democrat on the panel, said there was an "extraordinary spirit of cooperation" in drafting the bill. But he added that some Democrats voted against the budget agreement because "our feeling was that this was no time for a tax cut."
Senators from both parties offered 110 amendments to the bill, including five that would raise the federal tax on cigarettes.
Senate Finance Committee members met in closed session through the afternoon trying to pare down the number of amendments that will be considered.

The bill included $53 billion over five years in tax increases and revenue raisers, mainly from aviation taxes. The airline ticket tax would be extended but the rate reduced to 7.5 percent from 10 percent for flights in rural areas.
The bill would repeal the $6 departure tax and impose a 10 percent tax on the portion of the international ticket price attributable to flights in U.S. airspace.
Senators from states with major airports said the aviation tax proposals would hurt the airline and tourism industries.

Sen. Phil Gramm, a Texas Republican, likened the international ticket tax proposal to "putting a cover charge at a department store," saying it might discourage tourism to the United States in favour of another country.
"The Canadians ought to be outside handing out tourist literature," Gramm said.

The biggest piece of the proposed tax legislation would be $81 billion for a $500-per-child tax credit for children under 17. If the child is aged 13 to 16, the tax credit must be deposited in an IRA-type account earmarked for education.

Roth's bill provided a tax credit for college tuition, cut the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from a maximum 28 percent for individuals, and allowed married couples to exclude from taxes up to $500,000 of gain from selling a home.
The threshold at which the estate tax is imposed would be gradually raised to $1 million from the current $600,000 and the bill would expand Individual Retirement Accounts.
Democrats and the White House have raised more objections to the House bill than the Senate version, and speculation has begun over what type of bill President Clinton would sign.
If tax legislation were unchanged from the House version, "I predict the president will veto the bill," House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri said.
Democrats say Republican tax breaks favour the wealthy, and Republicans say Democrats were trying to increase welfare.

"The issue is clear. They (Republicans) take from the working poor, give to the middle class and what's left they passed on to the wealthiest," Representative Charles Rangel, the senior Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, said.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich spoke against Clinton Administration efforts to give the child tax credit to people who owe no income taxes and therefore would receive money from the government. "In a tax cut bill the focus ought to be on helping taxpayers," Gingrich said.
"At the end of the day, I believe the president will sign the bill," he added.
